items.followUp: Write four properties of cathode rays.

rubric.why: Identifies the positive nature of canal rays.
rubric.description: Canal rays consist of positively charged particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that canal rays are positively charged or consist of positive ions.

rubric.why: States their straight-line motion.
rubric.description: Canal rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Shows the direction of their deflection in an electric field.
rubric.description: They are deflected towards the negative plate, opposite to cathode rays.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the direction of deflection or that it is opposite to cathode rays.

rubric.why: Distinguishes canal rays from cathode rays, whose properties are independent of the gas used.
rubric.description: Their mass or charge-to-mass ratio depends on the gas in the discharge tube.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that their properties or charge-to-mass ratio depend on the gas used.

modelAnswer: Canal rays consist of positively charged particles (positive ions).
They travel in straight lines.
They are deflected towards the negative plate and in a direction opposite to cathode rays.
Their properties, including their charge-to-mass ratio, depend on the nature of the gas in the discharge tube.

items.followUp: Write five physical properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: Identifies the lustrous appearance of metals.
rubric.description: Metals are generally lustrous (shiny).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that metals are lustrous or shiny.

rubric.why: Identifies the ability of metals to be beaten into sheets.
rubric.description: Metals are malleable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Identifies the ability of metals to be drawn into wires.
rubric.description: Metals are ductile.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Identifies their electrical conductivity.
rubric.description: Metals are good conductors of electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that metals conduct electricity well.

rubric.why: Identifies their thermal conductivity.
rubric.description: Metals are good conductors of heat.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that metals conduct heat well.

modelAnswer: Metals are generally lustrous, or shiny.
Metals are malleable and can be beaten into thin sheets.
Metals are ductile and can be drawn into wires.
Metals are good conductors of electricity.
Metals are good conductors of heat.

items.followUp: Define solubility and explain why oil does not dissolve in water, giving an example of a solvent in which oil dissolves.

rubric.why: Defines solubility in terms of the maximum amount that dissolves.
rubric.description: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for expressing the maximum amount of solute that dissolves.

rubric.why: Includes the solvent quantity and conditions needed for a meaningful solubility value.
rubric.description: The maximum amount is specified for a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning a given amount of solvent and a specified temperature.

rubric.why: Explains that dissolution depends on interactions between solute and solvent particles.
rubric.description: Solubility depends on the interaction or attraction between solute and solvent particles; substances with similar properties tend to dissolve in one another.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the role of solute–solvent attraction or stating that like dissolves like.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of solute dissolving in a solvent.
rubric.description: For example, sodium chloride dissolves in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct solute–solvent example.

modelAnswer: Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature.
Dissolution depends on the interaction or attraction between solute and solvent particles; generally, like dissolves like.
For example, ionic sodium chloride dissolves in polar water because of the attraction between the ions and water molecules.

items.followUp: Calculate the molecular mass of carbon dioxide, CO₂. (C = 12 u, O = 16 u)

rubric.why: Uses the correct atomic masses and atom counts for water.
rubric.description: Molecular mass of H₂O = 2(1 u) + 16 u.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct calculation using two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

rubric.why: Gives the correct molecular mass with a unit.
rubric.description: Molecular mass of H₂O = 18 u (18 amu).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct final value with an appropriate unit.

modelAnswer: Given: H = 1 u and O = 16 u.
Molecular mass of H₂O = 2(H) + 1(O).

items.followUp: Define a formula unit and give the formula unit of magnesium chloride.

rubric.why: States that a formula unit represents the simplest ratio of ions in an ionic compound.
rubric.description: A formula unit is the simplest whole-number ratio of ions in an ionic compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this definition or its equivalent.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of an ionic compound and its formula unit.
rubric.description: For example, NaCl is the formula unit of sodium chloride.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example.

modelAnswer: A formula unit is the simplest whole-number ratio of ions in an ionic compound.
For example, NaCl is the formula unit of sodium chloride.

items.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of the Ca²⁺ ion in shells.

rubric.why: Recognises that the chloride ion has gained one electron from a neutral chlorine atom.
rubric.description: Cl⁻ has 18 electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the correct total number of electrons.

rubric.why: Gives the correct electronic configuration for 18 electrons.
rubric.description: Electronic configuration of Cl⁻ is 2,8,8 (or 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either correct shell or subshell configuration.

modelAnswer: A neutral chlorine atom has 17 electrons, so Cl⁻ has 18 electrons.
Electronic configuration of Cl⁻ = 2,8,8.

items.followUp: Describe Thomson’s model of the atom and explain why the atom is electrically neutral in this model.

rubric.why: States the central idea of the plum pudding model.
rubric.description: The atom was described as a sphere of positive charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the positively charged sphere.

rubric.why: States how electrons are arranged and explains the neutral atom model.
rubric.description: Electrons are embedded in the sphere; their negative charge balances the positive charge, making the atom neutral.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning embedded electrons or the balance of positive and negative charge.

modelAnswer: According to Thomson’s plum pudding theory, the atom is a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it.
The total positive charge balances the total negative charge of the electrons, so the atom is electrically neutral.

items.followUp: State the general trend of atomic radius across a period and down a group.

rubric.why: Gives the general period trend in electron affinity.
rubric.description: Electron affinity generally increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction across a period.

rubric.why: Gives the general group trend in electron affinity.
rubric.description: Electron affinity generally decreases down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction down a group.

modelAnswer: Across a period, electron affinity generally increases from left to right.
Down a group, electron affinity generally decreases.
